ray-dalio.limitations: Searched for political access, donations, government-linked benefit and Bridgewater-specific state dealings; only the items above were read. Wikipedia lists him as independent and records no donations; that is not a donations search of FEC records. No claim is made about China-related dealings beyond the article’s statement of a 2020 foundation gift. hussain-sajwani.reviewDepth: Narrow source-led review; not independently editorially reviewed
hussain-sajwani.period: Trump Organization partnership from 2010s; US pledge announced 2025-01-07
hussain-sajwani.summary: Sajwani is a long-time business partner of the Trump Organization and was publicly presented by Trump with a $20 billion US data-centre pledge in January 2025. The pages read document access and a licensing relationship, but not a state benefit or favour in return; the earlier promised deals did not materialise.
hussain-sajwani.mechanism: Trump-brand licensing partnership and presidential-level access; no preferential benefit established

support.text: AP reports Trump announcing DAMAC’s $20 billion US data-centre investment and notes that DAMAC built a Trump-branded golf club in Dubai and paid a multimillion-dollar licensing fee to the Trump Organization. AP says Sajwani was seen at Mar-a-Lago after the election and that the pledge suggests investors close to Trump can profit from the relationship. Trump said he wants investments of $1 billion or more to move quickly through environmental review.

In January 2017 Trump said he had turned down a $2 billion Dubai deal offered by Sajwani. DAMAC said that several property proposals had been discussed and rejected. Ethics experts quoted by NBC raised conflict-of-interest concerns about presidential family business ties.

counter.text: AP says the promised $2 billion in deals after the 2016 election never materialised and a planned Trump-named course was dropped; DAMAC’s data-centre arm had no US sites at the time. The article reports no regulatory favour and no critic responses, so it supports the commercial relationship but not a state benefit.
counter.source: Associated Press via WDIV ClickOnDetroit: limits

counter.text: Sajwani said after his 2016 discussions that he is not involved in political issues, according to NBC.

hussain-sajwani.limitations: Historical Egypt matter (a 2011 in-absentia sentence over a land purchase, suspended after a 2013 settlement) appears only in a Wikipedia summary and was not verified against primary or news sources, so it is not used as support. The review did not locate evidence on Dubai or Emirati state benefits, or on any US policy outcome favouring DAMAC after 2025. A licensing fee paid to the Trump Organization is a corporate commercial arrangement; it is not by itself a benefit to Sajwani from the state. This is a narrow review, not exoneration: absence of a documented mechanism in the sources read does not mean none exists.

shahid-khan.reviewDepth: Narrow source-led review; not independently editorially reviewed
shahid-khan.period: Jacksonville stadium agreement 2024–2025; inaugural donation reported 2017
shahid-khan.summary: The Jacksonville stadium agreement commits large city funds to a team-owned franchise, a conventional local public subsidy for which the council gave public approval; Khan separately gave $1 million to a 2017 presidential inaugural committee. Nothing read links the donation to the stadium deal or shows leverage beyond ordinary stadium-subsidy negotiation.
shahid-khan.mechanism: Public stadium financing for team lease; separate 2017 inaugural donation; no linkage established

support.text: PFT reports the city and Jaguars each commit $625 million to a $1.25 billion project, plus $150 million from the city for preparation, a new 30-year lease, and Khan covering cost overruns and day-to-day operations. The city funds its share from a capital-plan shift and an existing half-penny sales tax.

The council approved 14-1 on 25 June 2024. The lone no vote cited city finances, construction practice and the sales-tax plan; residents criticised separating the community-benefits agreement from the stadium deal.
support.kind: Local criticism of the public share

support.text: Bond Buyer reports a $355 million city bond sale in 2025 with $145 million for stadium reconstruction, repaid mainly from sales tax, state revenue sharing and utilities service taxes.
Sports Illustrated, citing an FEC disclosure, reports Khan donated $1 million to the Trump inaugural committee, alongside several other NFL owners.
support.access: Page summary reviewed via fetch tool

counter.text: The stadium terms make Khan responsible for overruns and operations, and the council vote was public and near-unanimous. The articles do not connect the Jacksonville deal to any donation or private favour; stadium subsidies are common and contested across the league.

Wikipedia records Khan publicly criticising Trump’s 2017 immigration ban and backing some economic policies while opposing social ones. Inauguration donations by many owners are not alone evidence of influence.
counter.access: Page summary reviewed via fetch tool; secondary summary, not a primary record

shahid-khan.limitations: Jaxdailyrecord pages on the 2021 hotel incentives package were not readable (HTTP 403), so no claim about that package is made. Not read: lobbying disclosures, council member donations from Khan or his companies, and any state-level benefits. The public-subsidy evidence is good on facts but is a standard local-policy transaction; it was not enough, with the thin political evidence, to assign a rubric. This is a narrow review, not exoneration: absence of a documented mechanism in the sources read does not mean none exists.

jaime-gilinski-bacal.reviewDepth: Narrow source-led review; not independently editorially reviewed
jaime-gilinski-bacal.period: Campaign loans reported (earlier cycle undated; 2026 runoff); GEA takeover 2021–2024
jaime-gilinski-bacal.summary: A Colombian investigative profile reports that Gilinski’s bank lent a presidential candidate roughly COP 5,000 million, and a 2026 report says GNB Sudameris lent about COP 17,500 million to a runoff campaign. Bank lending to campaigns is regulated rather than prohibited, no electoral authority has been reported to have examined the 2026 loan, and neither source establishes a state benefit in return.
jaime-gilinski-bacal.mechanism: Bank lending to campaigns; reported but undocumented political proximity; no benefit established

support.text: La Silla Vacía’s profile states that the bank financed almost all of Gustavo Petro’s second-round campaign with a COP 5,000 million loan, and that it also financed him in 2010. The profile does not clearly state the election year, and says rumours of closeness to Petro run through an associate, Álex Vernot. The reporting is the outlet’s own and is not sourced further.
support.source: La Silla Vacía: Quién es quién, Jaime Gilinski Bacal
support.access: Page read via fetch summary; update date September 2023; loan year ambiguous

support.text: Rio Times, citing La Silla Vacía, reports a GNB Sudameris loan of COP 17,500 million (about US$4.4 million) to Abelardo de la Espriella’s runoff campaign. The campaign declined to answer questions; the Gilinski group had made no public statement.
support.source: The Rio Times (citing La Silla Vacía)
support.kind: Reported campaign loan; attributed to the bank group
support.access: Secondary report of another outlet’s reporting; loan date not stated

counter.text: The Rio Times article says bank lending to campaigns is lawful in Colombia and regulated, that no electoral authority had examined this loan, and that it attributes the loan to the bank, not to Jaime Gilinski personally; it frames the concern as political proximity, not legality.
counter.source: The Rio Times: limits of evidence

counter.text: The family’s multi-company takeover bids for Grupo Sura and Grupo Nutresa were regulated tender offers; Jaime and Gabriel Gilinski resigned from the GNB Sudameris board in February 2022 to join those companies’ boards and avoid a conflict of interest. No political favour is alleged in the page.

jaime-gilinski-bacal.limitations: The two campaign-loan reports point to different candidates and cycles and the earlier one has an unclear year; the maintainer should not attribute both to the same race. Superintendencia and Petro-era regulatory decisions affecting his banks were searched but nothing was read about them. Personal versus bank-group conduct is not separated in the reporting. No finding, allegation of wrongdoing or sanction is reported in any page read. This is a narrow review, not exoneration: absence of a documented mechanism in the sources read does not mean none exists.
